utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Any problems with interpretation? Let me know. I notice the Defence teams are practically full force. Not so for the Prosecution. I see as the week approaches the end, you're left alone, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. McCloskey, today, is unaccompanied by any of his assistants. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. We do have an addition to our Defence team, Anika Mulder. She's sitting in the back right now, by Helen. She's a case manager. Just wanted to let you all know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Meek. And welcome, ma'am. Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to inform the Chamber that Mr. David Josse has been appointed co-counsel in this case, and the gentleman is seated to my right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for pointing out that he is seated to your right. We knew of his appointment and we have seen him before. I thank you, Mr. Krgovic. Any preliminaries? I see none. One preliminary. We were handed this before we entered the courtroom. This is something that is prepared by the Prosecution or by the Defence? Could we have that information?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We prepared that on your request, I believe, a couple of weeks ago. We will provide you a more detailed document that will have some of the other heavy equipment and things, but I think you mentioned specifically the rifles that are most applicable, and I -- that's our best judgement of most of the applicable rifle weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And I take it that this was done with the knowledge and consent of the Defence teams?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I handed them out, the documents, at the same time, and I'm sure they all remembered your request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just, for the record, I'm saying this not because I had any thoughts but simply to -- for the record, that they are being received by the Trial Chamber with all transparency. You don't mean to tender it as an exhibit, or do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think later on it's probably a good idea, as we get the other military equipment put together in a more complete binder. The Defence has most of the photos and the material from our previous exhibits, but we wanted to get better quality and put it in a packet, which -- I think it is a good idea. As you also know, we've provided you and everyone informally with a map book, and how you want to handle that formally is another good question, because there is another map book that I think would be helpful as well that's on its way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you so much. So I suggest we would mark it for identification for the time being. Judge Kwon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, let's mark it for identification, and later on we'll decide what to do with it, whether it will remain in the records and become an exhibit or whether it will be substituted by something more comprehensive. Thank you. So the next thing is, we were made aware earlier on in the day that you had filed a response to an application -- to a motion filed earlier on by Mr. Trbic or by his so-called, described, quasi amicus curiae, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. We have handed down the decision. I just wanted to inform you that we were fully aware of the contents of your response. Sorry to disappointment you, but the case goes on. The other thing is, Mr. Ostojic, in the course of the last sitting that was the day before yesterday, while Mr. Ruez was testifying, you made or you tabled orally a request for the -- for the witness to be asked to make available the so-called working papers, which in the transcript may, at some time, been referred to as working statements. We promised you that we will hand down a decision before we continue with the testimony today, and this is our decision: We are guided, first of all, by what is included in -- what is stated in Rule 70(A) of the Rules, namely, that notwithstanding the provisions much Rules 66 and 67 which deal with disclosure, reports, memoranda or other internal documents prepared by a party, its assistants or representatives in connection with the investigation or preparation of a case are not subject to disclosure or notification under those Rules. Mr. Ruez at the time was a member of the Prosecution team, carrying out investigations for the Prosecution. Today he is no longer part of the Prosecution team, but that doesn't change the nature of these working -- so-called working papers. If they are not subject to disclosure, equally they are not subject also to production, compulsory production here during the testimony of the person who kept them or may have been involved in their preparation. So that disposes of your request. Mr. Zivanovic, unless there is any other preliminary business to transact, I see, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Before I continue with my cross-examination, I would just like to indicate that the last photo that was shown to the witness, which was the photo -- the aerial photo of the town of Bratunac, was number 2103, and that is photo number 272 from the overall collection of photos.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ruez, I wanted to ask you something about the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment, one moment, one moment. I don't want to get confused with this, but something tells me in my mind that 2103 is not correct. I think 2103 is the CD that the Prosecution wanted to -- or sought to introduce and which you have objected to. Can someone help me, please? My recollection is the following, Mr. Zivanovic, but Mr. McCloskey, please, and your case manager, try to help me. To me, if I remember well, and I stand corrected -- to be corrected, 2103 is the CD containing the 271 photos. The additional photo of Bratunac, which, according to Mr. McCloskey, is a better photo with also more detail included, was not tendered in substitution of the photo that was already in 2103. That's not how I understood it to be. It was tendered separately. If I am wrong, please tell me so. But I need to be guided here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Especially if you are objecting as a team -- as a group, you are objecting to the admission of 2103. So I don't know. I will not say more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You had it just -- just right, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, I think so, yes. So let's -- Mr. Ostojic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may add to the debate. If an exhibit is introduced for identification, we -- although we object to that exhibit, we would like to at least expand on that exhibit without waiving our right and indicating that we may accept the exhibit. If we object, it shouldn't preclude us from inquiring about the exhibit because we hope to at least explore why we further think it's inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely. Definitely. You must have misunderstood what I said. What I was saying is, I was just opening Mr. Zivanovic's right, that if he thought it was part of 2103, he must keep also in mind that that was, in its totality, a document that you were objecting to. So it needed to be careful, what -- how to put it. But otherwise, of course you are entitled to cross-examine the witness on each one of those 271 pages, without prejudicing your objection that you raised earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So what's the number of that map, 2104?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey. Mr. McCloskey, did you add another page, an extra page, to 2103 when you tendered the document, or did you tender it separately from 2103?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we thought it would be simpler to get it 272, but it doesn't really matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So it's page 272 of 2103, and we'll go ahead, we'll proceed along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, I won't ask you any more questions about the photo. I would like to direct your attention to the intercepts. Before me I have a statement of yours which is part of the RDS collection, and the number is 02008676. On our list, this is marked as 1D00012. Since this document is classified as confidential, I believe we should move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go into private session -- private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to provide an explanation. The document that I presented was marked "Confidential". The Prosecution marked the document as confidential so this is why I asked to be in private session. That was the only reason I did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's not necessary in this context, but we appreciate the concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you to look at the following four pages of these documents. They are actually the attachments which you signed for. This is the third -- second, third, fourth, and fifth page. Did you have a look at those pages? I don't know if you've had an opportunity to look.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a perfect look, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just want to make sure that you are looking at the English version, Mr. Ruez. English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's not but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You've got it, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise the precise way that Sevko Tihic was accustomed to do his logs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Page 2, you will agree, is nothing but a list of documents, a list of the material that should have been handed over to you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But not the material itself.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The material goes with the document at the time we sign it. It's a normal procedure. So if I had that list, the material that went with it would -- handed over that day, I would think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But that material was not specified, it doesn't say exactly what it contains. Or maybe you had controlled the material and collated the material with the log.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, most of the time either the things went on request, or the process was that people of the team, together with officers of 2nd Corps, would go through the material and it was then specified what was of interest for us. Then the 2nd Corps prepared the log of this material. Upon return in The Hague, based on this list, all these items were entered into evidence at the Evidence Unit, so they were given a registration number and a description of what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In any case, on the 10th of March, when you provided your previous statement, you still did not have the material that had been handed over to you listed and specified, because I see that in the last paragraph of your previous statement, you indicate that the material is not specified, that it is -- that it is a large quantity of an unspecified material.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We should have to look at that last sentence in my confidential memo, but this -- I take it, as you say, yes, this is absolutely possible, since, as far as I remember, it was a bunch of computer printouts and they were considered as one item and would have been, let's say, registered in more details once analysed here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. And now I would like to ask you something about an interview of yours -- actually, a conversation, as it is indicated. This is document number 1D0006, and the B/C/S version is 0307-4564; and 0307-3101 is the English translation of this document. I suppose that you know what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is not a conversation. This is, I think, my hearing at the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's how it's been translated.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Translations sometimes create fuzziness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe there's a French version that may actually help him a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, it's fine.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No this "conversation" is the transcript of my hearing at the National Assembly in front of the Common Commission of Ministry of Defence and Ministry of Foreign Affairs. It was an information mission of a parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to one sentence in this interview which is in paragraph 3, the second sentence thereof. In the B/C/S translation, it reads: "The contents of my presentation have to be taken with a pinch of salt because it has not been presented to the Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia." Are these your words, sir?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will need to tell you what I relate when I say that. It's not for my entire hearing, it's for the, let's say, maybe the three first paragraphs which are related to ethnic cleansing starting in 1992. And there was no -- there was, I think, a trial going on in 2001. But anyhow, this elements related to the 1992 situation. It was not part of the investigation, and this is why I say that: "The first things I'm going to tell you are not part of the investigation. All the rest will be, indeed, results of the investigation." You will even note in a later paragraph that there is either my mistake, either a transcription mistake: Paragraph 5 starts with "In April 1995 in Bratunac"; one should read here "In April 1992 in Bratunac," not 1995. It's the only mistake I have seen in this transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't say then that this was relative only to the year 1992 and that's why the contents were not reliable. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The contents is reliable. There is one mistake on the date. In Bratunac, Vuk Karadzic school event of 1992 was in 1992, not in 1995, as written on this transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you that. I'm asking you about the sentence. You didn't say that this caveat is relative to only the year 1992. You've told us that now but you didn't say it then, did you?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought I would be understood when I said that, since the reason why I was called to parliament is that it's a well-known fact I investigated the events from 1995, not from 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to draw your attention to a report by Professor Richard Wright about exhumations in Eastern Bosnia in 1998. The report is dated 12 May 1999. It is on the 65 ter list as B00666, and the ERN number is 00848214. I would like to show you pages 28 and 29 of this report. I apologise. Can you move on to page 29, please? This is the page that I actually wanted, page 29. Yes. Could you please look at the bottom part of this page. Can you look at the table, please. Let me remind you: This is a table reflecting the watches that were found in various locations during this exhumation, and in the first column you will see the locations where the watches were found and in the last column you will see the dates when these wrist watches displayed at the moment of the exhumation. Can we move on to the next page, please. There are two more watches here, the rest of the table. And now I would like to draw your attention to the third paragraph of these findings in which Professor Wright says: "Jean-Rene Ruez, the investigator for the ICTY, tells me that executions at the suspected primary graves took place on the evening of Friday, 14th July 1995." Could you please reply by saying just yes or no when I ask you: Is this what you told Professor Wright?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question to you is this: On several occasions you inspected all of the places where the detainees had been held, especially gyms and sports halls; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In any of these places, and I'm going to specify, the gym in Orahovac, did you ever measure that hall, either you personally or any member of your team?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What about Pilica, the Kula school, actually, near Pilica?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not do any -- we did not even enter -- yes, sorry, we entered the gym. We did no specific work on the Pilica school, since an NGO had started renovation in that place as soon as the end of 1996, if I recall well. So there was a brand new gym and new classrooms. And the other point is that we do not consider that school as a crime scene due to the fact that we have no reports of physical abuse committed inside. So there was no necessity to go there in order to make a fine survey to collect whatever samples could be of interest for the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ruez, I'm coming to my last few questions that we should consider. You conducted this investigation on Srebrenica for five years and nine months; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: During that time, you had lots of conversations with many people. You contacted a number of institutions, the Bosnian authorities, the authorities of Republika Srpska. Would all that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: During your investigation, you must have formed an opinion on the events that had taken place there.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what one could call my personal speculations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, did you form any particular prejudices or antagonism towards any of the sides that you spoke to during your investigation?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You treated everybody equally, from the same point of view?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would summarise it by: No friends, no foe situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now look at the last document, which is 1D009 from our exhibit list. This is an interview that you yourself gave in April, 2001, after having left the Hague Tribunal. We have both a B/C/S and an English version of your interview. This interview was published in the newspaper called Monitor, which is published in Montenegro. It had two sequels, and I'm now going to draw your attention to the second part of this interview that was published on the 21st of April, 2001. I believe you have the translation of that interview before you?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to page 43 in the B/C/S version, and in the English version this is on page 6. Immediately below the circled text, in other words, somewhat towards the middle of that page, below the text that is encircled. Can you see that? To the journalist's question, you say: "It should be said that the Bosniaks had reason to conceal that the zone was not demilitarised and that, as they claim, the army did not aid the 28th Division in the enclave. There is a third thing that they want to hide, and that is the command and control of the Main Staff of the BH army over the 28th Division, if its members committed crimes, and the Serbs claim they did from 1992 to 1995." Is this a good translation of your words? Is this what you said?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So for this one, the opposite of the previous document, this one is a real conversation. It was even held in a restaurant. But yes, these are the words that I used.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that you base the legitimacy for this in the fact that nobody was duty-bound to provide you with any information that might have incriminated themselves, and that's why you believed that it was legitimate for the Bosnian authorities to act the way they did. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly would not say, if I understood you well, that their behaviour was legitimate. To me it is not. But I can understand the concerns that the people had in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, I suppose that you find the reasons for that in the fact that they did not want to reveal information that might have been detrimental for them.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, this is basic behaviour for whoever or whatever institution or government who has something to hide. He collaborates with you on the aspects of interest for him but certainly not on the other ones. It's human nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And this is also customary and can be applied to individuals as well.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you, as an experienced investigator, have a lot of understanding for that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would not put it like this. What I have to say also is that I was in no way in charge of the investigation against the Muslim side or the 28th Division. My task was to investigate on the crimes that followed the fall of the enclave. But it's a fact, also, that being a member of a prosecutor, it takes time to gain trust with your contacts in such circumstances, and this time to gain trust is also an explanation for some slowliness that we can regret on the Prosecution side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, what I am saying, as an experienced investigator, you found it understandable that people behaved the way they did, by concealing information from you if they thought that that information would be detrimental for them. I'm sure that you had encountered that in your previous practice, before you even joined the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is asked and answered, and also pretty fundamental.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to the next question, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I shall move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can the witness please look at the -- page 43, the first column at the end, the last paragraph in the B/C/S version, which, in the English translation, can be found on page 5 - just a moment; please bear with me - the last paragraph on page 5. To the journalist's questions, you say: "One thing astounded me. There is an astonishing gulf between what professional officers deem professional honour, duties and activities and the conduct and the mentality of more than 90 percent of the VRS officers we met. They behave like thugs hiding everything, even the most obvious. They don't accuse others, because most of them had not reached that point yet, but most of them would as soon as they felt the smell of prison, even the most modern one, with the most decent guards. Men without honour. They behave like petty thieves, like children caught with their hands in jam jars, totally afraid of the possible repercussions." Were these your words?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Zivanovic. It's five minutes to our break, so I suggest we have the break now. And since we have some matters to discuss, the break will be of 30 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's your turn, Mr. Ostojic or Mr. Meek. I don't know who is going to cross-examine the witness. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ruez. How are you?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you a couple of questions, and I plan not to be repetitive, and with the Court's ruling, I will reduce my questioning, based on the Court's earlier ruling regarding your mission statements, e-mails, et cetera, but I may have just a couple points of clarification on that, understanding the Court's ruling. Sir, if I may, by way of personal background, what's your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 20th of February, 1961.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, you testified in your direct examination that when you were working for the French police, that that department was subdivided into five groups, I think you said, the police order, the public security, general information services, counter-intelligence, and judicial police; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm curious about a couple of things. While you were working with the French police, how would a subordinate in one of the other departments, let's say public order or counter-intelligence, referring to you, someone who's working in the judicial police, being a superintendant dant in the judicial police, how would they call you?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would call me Monsieur Commissaire.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Even those people in the other departments, those five, they were not directly subordinate to you because you were the superinten dant of the judicial police; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And they would still call you Mr. Superintendant; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those of a rank under this one would call me like this. In Paris this is a specific expression that is -- but it's specific to Paris. It is patron, that means boss.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In Serbian would it be like Chef?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me ask you this, sir: During your seven-year tenure with the French police, you worked exclusively for, basically, the Office of the Prosecution; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And during your six years with the ICTY, you've worked exclusively with the Office of the Prosecution; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Have you ever worked for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's talk a little bit about your tenure at the OTP, if we may. I think you told us you started basically on the 7th of April, 1995, and ended on the 7th of April, 2001; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, before you started the Srebrenica investigation, were you briefed or given an overview of what it is you were going to investigate?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was not -- no such briefing. In fact, I already said that the initial mission was to check press rumours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So, is it fair to summarise that your investigation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you kindly make breaks between questions and answers for the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the interpreter is a hundred per cent right. The one at fault most is yourself, Mr. Ostojic. So if you could -- because Mr. Ruez is taking a little bit of a pause, but you're not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I apologise, Your Honour. I will. With the time constraint, I'm trying to rush through it, if you don't mind. But thank you, and I will try to pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I could summarise, and you correct me if I'm wrong, sir, your initial investigation started as a result of "press rumours"?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, once these rumours did hit the Office of the Prosecutor, the Prosecutor decided that someone should be sent in the area and start investigating the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm trying to get to. The Prosecutor then sent you, or you, being in charge of the investigation, decided that it would be worthy of an investigation and went on your own?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There is nothing I would have done on my own. I was tasked to go there and assess the situation; this, for sure, in order for the OTP to decide if an investigation should or not be opened on these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And who ultimately made that decision, you, that an investigation should be opened?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not me. This is the responsibility of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Were there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One other thing. I haven't heard the interpreters complain, but I'm sure that when you're moving the papers and the lectern, you're making a noise which would definitely hurt their ears, such as you're doing now. So if you could kindly switch off the microphone when you're moving papers or the lectern, I think you would help them, because it does hurt their ears and disturb them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll do that, Your Honour. It's just a little awkward. I'll do that, though. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you think it's more comfortable for you to sit down, please sit down. I think it would be easier because of your size.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, I would rather stand. But if you instruct me to sit down, I will, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez will not be intimidated by your size.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, were there any limitations or parameters placed on your investigation?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer would be no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you describe for us what was the breadth of the investigation initially?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I ask you to -- precisely what you mean by "the breadth of the investigation"?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sure. Thank you for that. If at any time you don't understand, I'll hopefully try to help you. What was the extent of your investigation initially?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The extent was to investigate on the crimes committed after the fall of Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So the press rumours, you've already concluded that crimes were committed, and you were going to investigate those crimes; is that correct? Is that the way I understand it?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, since the press people who were in that area, for many of them, since the beginning of the war, though they had no proof about what they were writing, were immediately writing that all the missing men were certainly already dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what was the initial goal, sir?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the initial goal was to try to find out what happened after the enclave was taken over by the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did, at any time, you investigate what happened before the enclave fell?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. This was not part of, let's call it, the mandate of this investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that might be precisely what I'm trying to understand better. What was the mandate? And did it have any restrictions? And forgive me if I'm wrong, but I thought you said there were no limitations on that mandate. So if you may clarify it for me, please.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The mandate being, at least as I understood it, to investigate the events that followed the fall of the enclave, the criminal events that followed the fall of the enclave. There was no limitation in the frame of that mandate. The investigation about what happened in the area between 1992 and 1995 was the topic of two separate investigations at the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That helps a little. Was the mandate narrowed further that you would investigate the crimes purportedly committed only by the Serbs, or were you to investigate the crimes committed by any party in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The victims of this investigation, being the Bosniak Muslims who were inside the enclave, this investigation was limited to the Bosniak victims. There were other investigations ongoing that were dealing with the aspect of the Serb victims in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you were not involved in that; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not involved in that, but if I came across information useful for other teams and investigations, I was taking what was available and I provided the investigation teams with the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, can you share with us the number of trips you made in Bosnia or in Srebrenica or in Tuzla as a result of your investigation for the six years that you were working as the investigator for the ICTY? And just -- I believe that you've already testified that the first visit was July 20th, 1995. So, if you could just chronologically list that out for me, it might help confine some of my questions.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would do it with pleasure, though I never made any summary of all these missions. If I take the year 1996, what I can say is that there was a mission in January, there was a mission in April, there was a mission in June, there was a mission in August. And I should go like this year by year. It would be hard to say. Some missions were for three weeks; others were for three days. I don't have a global survey of all this. It was a constant going back and return from The Hague to the mission area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, can you maybe help us? You've done a good job with 1996, and I think in 1995, is it one trip you made in 1995, July 20th?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. During all these years, I always tried to make sure we would at least arrive for the 1st of April in the area, and there were many number of -- I'm only talking about my missions. I would say approximately five missions a year. But once the team became what we could really call a team, then you would add the missions of the other team members. So it is a large number of missions, indeed, in that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so that you're clear, I'm only interested in your investigation that you did, not necessarily as a team.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I know we, the other day, had a little discussion about the use of the word "we" or "I" and the collective "we" if you will. I'm only interested in your physical presence and when you went to Srebrenica or Tuzla or to the various areas that you discussed in your direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Is there anything more that I have to add, then, to your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. When was your last visit? And we didn't hear anything about 1997 or 1998 or 1999 or 2000 or 2001. So there is a little bit more, if you can help me.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. It would be very hard, because -- let's slice the investigation in several pieces. The first step was mainly to conduct interviews in order to reconstruct the events, so this was mainly the topic of the missions for the years 1996, 1997, 1998, in terms of interviews of victims. But it continued until the end of also but at a smaller pace. 1996 was also the year where there was a need to find and process all the crime scenes, so this was done during the years 1996 and 1997. Then there was also the need to identify the locations of the main mass graves and later the secondary mass graves. This was done during the years 1997, 1998, and 1999. There was also a need for missions in order to check some aspects in connection with the trials. There was also an interview process of Bosnian Serb officers that started in 1999, continued in 2000, all this generating a certain number of missions. There was also the need for several missions that started, I think, in 1998, when we were conducting an operation of search and seizure of automatic weapons at the Bratunac and Zvornik Brigades and processing all this material. So that generated missions in 1998 and 1999. So aside giving you my binder of what we call the finance binder, because it's for administration, I would have a really hard time to reconstruct, on top of my memory, all these missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's fair. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Ruez. I thought I heard you say yesterday that you went back to the area last year. Did you go back after you left your employment with the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And now, can you tell us from April 7th, 2001, to last year, how often would you go back to the area?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My first return was in July/August 2001, where I accompanied a crew of two journalists in order to fulfil a promise that had been made to them by the Office of the Prosecutor prior to my departure. Then I returned in 2005, first to give a briefing in Srebrenica town on the request of the Outreach Programme of the Tribunal, and I returned also during that same summer with a French journalist who has an interest on this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's the extent of your return visits?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, do you agree with me that, as an investigator, in order to maintain your integrity and the reputation of the investigation, as well as the oath of office you may have taken, that you must do a thorough, objective, and complete examination of events; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, because sometimes we don't understand the meaning of certain words, I'm inviting you to tell me what your opinion, or what your definition, rather, is of the word "objective."

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see your point. "Objective" is the opposite of biased.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so we're talking about the same thing. I agree, and there are other definitions. Now, the term "investigation," do you know if that connotes to confirm or corroborate certain evidence, or does it mean to examine, without bias, certain evidence; and to gather all the evidence, good, bad, negative or positive, before you may reach a conclusion on a certain issue?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You say that in a better format that I could be able to do, but I buy your words.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, you're honestly very modest, because those are not my words, as you remember. In fact, in the prior testimonies, you've used those very words and you've shared with us that your first -- in fact, your first priority in the investigation was to confirm the stories about abuse and atrocities; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Confirm or infirm, assess the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And your second priority was to exhume the graves and gather physical evidence; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the third priority would be to find those culpable and accountable for those crimes and atrocities; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Totally correct, the three steps of this investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "confirm or infirm"?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I mean with that is that, if -- let's say the example of a witness who we will request for interview based on a summary of information that we received either from AID or from the War Crime Commission, based on the statement we would take from him, we would then either be willing to confirm his information by finding some forensics in connection with what he's saying or, due to inconsistencies or whatever other reason related to this witness, we would disregard this information because we would believe it is not worth being trusted, or we would investigate, again, that same situation, in order to make sure that we reject this witness for good reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not an investigator, but would it be fair to summarise that an investigator or a team leader, such as yourself, when you went out to interview various potential witnesses, that ultimately you would render an impression of whether or not you need to confirm or to disregard their testimony -- their evidence, I'm sorry, not their testimony.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's say that it's always the same thing. There's a pyramid of priorities to be done. If there is a possibility to check everything, everything would be checked. If, because of this pyramid of priorities, things have to be pushed aside, we had to push them aside.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What is that pyramid? I'm not that familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's say that if a witness reports to us a location where he saw three people being shot but we also have to go to another site where someone claims the dead count in the hundreds, we would give priority to assess the situation where the count of hundreds of dead rather than trying to find the location where we could eventually find three bodies. This is, unfortunately, the type of priorities we had to make in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't mean to interrupt. I thought you were finished. I'm not asking you to give me an example. I'm asking you to tell me what was the pyramid that you used when you would confirm witness's statements? Would you go out, for example, looking for other witnesses to corroborate that testimony? Would you go out on the field forensically to try to substantiate what those witnesses may have said?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Tell me more about this pyramid.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is exactly what you said at this moment. That was all the things that we -- not only that we had to do but that we did with these witnesses, but then the chronology of how to do it was based on the seriousness of the allegations that were made by these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, with respect to this priority number 1, I've categorised it "confirm the stories," and if I can briefly, not to recite your entire testimony in other cases, but for my learned colleague at the Office of the Prosecution, at Blagojevic trial, page 612, lines 23 through 25, I believe you said: "Priority number 1 was to interview witnesses and identify possible crime scenes that could then be analysed in order to corroborate their declarations." Do you remember giving that testimony?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirm the entire sentence. What I do not confirm is the way you categorise this step number 1, because I don't really appreciate the word "stories." It's confirm the testimonies. In fact, I call this the period of reconstruction of the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I truly, with all due respect, did not mean to categorise it anything different than you may have, so I will change that to "confirm or reconstruct the events." Is that fair enough?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, do you recall also in that Blagojevic trial telling the Honourable Judge Veselenko that your priority was -- number 1 priority, was that you could confirm the declarations of the various potential witnesses?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was absolutely a top priority, especially when knowing what these declarations were. Most of them were declarations of people having survived mass executions. So, yes, it was a top priority.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know the difference between the word "investigate" and the word "confirm"?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see your point. I see the point, but it's the same to me. If what we would find would confirm, it's part of the investigation. If it would not confirm, it would also be part of the investigation. When I say we need to confirm, it's either confirm or find elements that lead to reject the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, do you have a -- did you have a binder or a DVD or some mechanism where you would know, perhaps offhand, the list of witnesses that you had rejected as not being credible for one reason? Because I notice in the witness statements there's never an impression by any investigator of what they thought of a particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very simple answer: The ultimate stage of an investigation is to present the evidence in a courtroom. In a courtroom we show the information that is the result of leads that we have followed and that we, the Prosecutor, believes are positive. We are not exposing to the Court all the dead-ends in which we entered, nor did we expose the wrong leads we are sometimes taking -- taken. So, no, we don't have such a list. I have examples in my memory, but we never made such a list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Ostojic. Mr. Haynes, I saw you. Do you have a problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I really didn't want to interrupt, but I think everybody's LiveNote facility has crashed on the Defence side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see a technician working with Mr. Meek. We'll stop, if necessary, because it's important that you are all able to follow. Could you ask the technician whether a five-minute break -- I apologise to you, Mr. Ostojic, but this is something which is important for everyone. Is the problem solved, or not? Let's have a five-minute break, or longer if necessary. We will be outside wait -- I'm sorry, but if your colleagues cannot follow on the screen, that's not the ideal we should be aiming for. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I am told that everything is in working order now. I'll just check on mine, at least. It seems to be in working order. Any of the Defence teams encountering problems?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We're able to follow the proceedings. The other facilities that should be available will not be available for the remainder of the afternoon, but that's the best we can go so we'll get on with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which other facilities? Such as annotations?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Annotation, the issue of highlighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it can be done. At least on our side we can do it. I see, I see, I see. All right, okay. All right. Let's go ahead. I'm sure you will find a way of monitoring what is being said for future reference. Yes, Mr. Ostojic, you may proceed. And sorry, once more, for the interruption, but this was needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, right before the break we were discussing several concepts. Am I correct, although I'm not an investigator, that the point of an investigation to bring to a courthouse is to bring forth the truth. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on page 44, lines 15 through 18, just prior to our break, you said as follows, and I'll quote it, and I have a couple questions on this so bear with me, quote: "The ultimate goal of an investigation is to present the evidence in a courtroom. In a courtroom we show the information that is the result of leads that we have followed and that we, the Prosecutor, believes are positive." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. When you say that the Prosecutor believes are positive, aren't you, sir, really telling us that you're bringing forth evidence that you deem to be positive to your ultimate goal of convictions?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I mean with "positive" is our assessment that the situation we present is the truth, the reason why the Prosecutor decides to present it together with its evidence to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That helps a little. Are you familiar with the forensic or psychiatric term of "confirmatory bias"?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not in touch with many psychiatrists so I would not comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to comment on what you think about it. I'm asking if you've ever heard that use of that word or those words, "confirmatory bias," as it may relate to police officers investigating crimes or prosecutors prosecuting crimes? Have you ever heard that in your 13 years of experience? I don't know why it's funny.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I know where you want to go with this in advance. Yes, for sure I know what this means, "confirmatory bias."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Again, just so we're on the same page, why don't you describe for me what confirmatory bias is.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be the case for someone who is so much convinced that someone would be guilty that he would totally disregard anything that would get him out of this obsession. Is that fine with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, hopefully we'll have someone with a little more, with all due respect, expertise share what that is. But if that's your answer, I will accept it at this point. Sir, you testified previously today, in fact, when I was questioning you, that you initially got these press rumours because "they," meaning the press, were at the scene, were there in Srebrenica or Tuzla or wherever. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I interrupt you here. He never said so. In fact, the press reports, as he described them earlier on in his testimony, just were in a sense that there were a number of persons unaccounted for and that they -- the conclusion that was being reached in the press was that they had been killed. This is how he described it earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If it is, I stand corrected, Your Honour. That's not the point I'm trying to make. I just want to direct his attention to the press releases generally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what he stated earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You heard the President, and you said initially when I asked you about what you were briefed on, you mentioned press releases as a general category; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, are these the press releases from journalists who were at the scene as the events were unfolding in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these press releases would be available at the press office, when looking into the binder of press articles published in end of July 1995. These are the ones that prompted not my decision but the decision of the Prosecutor to send an investigator on the scene in order to assess the situation. You will have to check who wrote these articles and inquire on them. But as far as I know, the people who, at least I talked with, were people who were doing their work in that area since many years, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And those people you reference, are those journalists? Right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not interested so much in the articles. I'm interested in the methodology and the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- that the investigator in Srebrenica used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Both speakers are requested to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Both speakers are requested to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're doing again what we told you not to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And again I apologise. The break has given me additional energy, so I will try to maintain and follow your request, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any time you require further breaks, let us know, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And it was the journalists and the press releases that you or the Office of the Prosecutor received, that -- that initiated the investigation on the Srebrenica enclave after the fall of the enclave, as you've testified; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you worked -- you worked for the Office of the Prosecutor in the ICTY under a United Nations mandate; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At that same time, sir, isn't it true that there were United Nations personnel stationed in Srebrenica and in that area that you described during your direct, during the time period after the fall of Srebrenica in 1995?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, as an investigator who would do a complete and thorough and objective job, wouldn't it have been more prudent to talk to those UN personnel as opposed to follow leads from the press or journalists who were on the scene?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several steps in my answer: The first one is that we didn't follow the leads from the journalists who were on the scene, the scene being the area of Tuzla, not the area where the event happened. We later on -- indeed, each time a press article referred to a potential witness, we systematically approached that witness in order to check the information that was provided to the press. That's the first comment. There was another thing in your question? The UN personnel you referred to exited the area through Belgrade and then directly landed in the Netherlands. The interview of that personnel was the topic of an interview process that lasted for at least a one-year-long period of time, happening little mission after little mission. So this aspect was conducted. But more prudent to start with them? I would say no. The most prudent approach was first to identify among the key witnesses those who would still be serving in the army. Since the war was still ongoing, our concern was that they could be sent back to the front line and that we might, for the future, lose a valuable witness for the Prosecution. That was among the concerns.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Let me ask you: Did you, at any time in your investigation, seek to obtain the reports from United Nations personnel during the time of your initial or immediate, subsequent visits to the area?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did obtain all the records, not only the reports drafted by the UN soldiers to the UN but also to their own minister -- Ministry of Defence. As well did we receive all the situation reports of the United Nations military observers. So we got all that material, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Ostojic. It seems that we are having problems. I discovered a couple of minutes ago that I was disconnected. I tried to connect again. I was connected again. Now I was disconnected, and it is only now that I am connected again. Judge Prost has lost her connection completely. In the meantime -- are the Defence teams -- you have problems as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I lost mine but I've got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. If we can proceed, we'll try to concentrate on what appears on -- at least you should have the transcript scrolling on one monitor, if not on the other. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed. And if we encounter problems, then we'll try and do something about it, rather than stopping again. I mean, otherwise, Mr. Ostojic will come back with more energy and it will be no fun after that. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, may you answer my question: When? We were discussing the UN files, et cetera. When did you obtain those?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In several episodes, in fact. What we got first was the situation reports from the UNMOs. I think we got that during the summer 1995. And then it was a more lengthy process with the Dutch military. It took some longer time. But the requests were fulfilled when they were launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't quite understand what that means, "the requests were fulfilled when launched." Immediately? Or did it take some time?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means when the requests were made, they were fulfilled. But they were not made at once. It was a process that was several times interrupted. One interruption, for example, was in 1996 that the OTP was running out of money and couldn't pay any more the missions for the investigators. So there was one mission to be conducted in Assen, in the Netherlands, that was called off. Those are things that happen during the course of an investigation here at the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just give me a date when you thought it was completed. In what year? That's what I'm looking for. 1999? 1998?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say the date of full completion, 1998 -- 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Beginning or late 1998; do you know?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could be end of 1997 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: End of 1997, beginning 1998; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, how about the Bratunac Brigade? When did you, as the lead investigator on the Srebrenica trial, seek the records from the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure you have a very precise date of that seizure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's fine. Let me refresh your recollection, so we can move it along.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sorry, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's not a memory test. So thank you for that. I have that it was approximately December of 1998 that the first request for a seizure of the Bratunac Brigade was made; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, together with the one of the Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: My next question: With regard to the Zvornik Brigade, it was done simultaneously in the summer of 1998.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was also simultaneous separation, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Approximately in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers pause a moment between questions and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Ostojic and Mr. Ruez, please slow down and allow a short pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Again, I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Share with me the dates in which you, as the lead investigator, initially requested and obtained the Drina Corps documents.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: These ones were obtained in two different moments in time. One part of the archives was seized during the search you are referring to, and the rest of these archives, at least part of the rest, was provided to the Office of the Prosecutor after my departure in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. How about the military personnel files of the military --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, would you repeat your question. The microphone was not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The microphone is on, but I'll repeat it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your microphone was off so the interpreters couldn't catch what you were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Tell me when the Office of the Prosecution, or you as the investigator, requested military personnel files on military men who were with the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that we made such a request. The files I'm talking about were seized, not requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me, if you will, whether or not you ever seized the military personnel files of military soldiers in the VRS, and when that was.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, military files, I mean personnel files of military personnel were seized both at the headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade and also at the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about those of the Main Staff? Would they also be located, the military personnel files of those individuals, in the Bratunac and Zvornik Brigades?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think they would be part of these archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When did you request those such documents, if at all?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. If such a request was done, I would think it was done probably in the year 2000, or possibly even after my departure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, going back to our little -- complete, thorough, and objective, when did you first obtain the military records from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina involving specifically the events as perhaps they -- from their perspective, transpired in Srebrenica 1995?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know any -- of any document that would indicate what the view of the Bosnian Serb army was about these events. The only document I know about is the document that was compiled by the government of the Republika Srpska, dated, I think, in 2001, where indeed the Republika Srpska --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that. I don't mean to interrupt you, if we can just move along. It was my fault because I used the wrong term, "view." I don't mean necessarily their view. What I'm looking for is, when did you, as the Office of the Prosecutor, and you as an investigator, seek and seize documents from the ABiH in connection with the events that unfolded from July 11th through the 17th of 1995. We'll get to the other issues a little later, hopefully?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't get that you were talk from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was thinking about the other. No, again, I had no -- I mean, for the sake of this investigation, I had no immediate interest in what happened between 1992 and 1995, so I was not looking for documents about this period of time, on both sides I didn't -- that was not the topic of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I heard that and I understood it before, actually, and now. I'm really looking for, and we can confine my questions to that period, as I thought I said in my question, July 11th through the 17th, 1995. During that period of time, did you ever seize or request documents from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina for documents that they may have in their possession from their military men or women who were at or near that enclave at that time? When did you request those documents, if at all?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand better. Yes, it was requested in the first days of our arrival. What we were receiving at the initial stage, and this is anyhow what we got, were summaries of debriefings that were made by the police and by the army; the police dealing with the civilian refugees; the army interviewing their own people about this. And we received the -- some summaries of the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I thought you said the other day that you, the investigator, were looking for "key" witnesses; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that when going through the few hundreds of summarised statements we had access to, we separated them in several groups, one group being witnesses of events that happened during the "evacuation/deportation"; the other group were - sorry - witnesses who could talk about the events in Potocari; a third group was witnesses who we named, and you will understand, the "wood walkers", those who went through the forest; and the last and the most tiny group, witnesses who claimed having survived the mass execution. So, to answer your question, the people we call "key" witnesses were a focused group of people who had what seems to be the prima facie, very important information, to communicate to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Explain to us, if you will, how it is that you came upon to these key witnesses who had important information to explain to you? Did someone bring them to you? Did you, for lack of an example, put an advertisement in the paper seeking these people? Or how is it you came upon them with so many people in the area?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I already talked about that aspect, but I will repeat it. Our sources of information during this summer 1995 was: One, the summarised statements taken by AID; two, statements, but not many of them, taken by UN personnel; three, statements taken by the War Crime Commission; four, the spreading among refugees in refugee camps of questionnaires prepared by the OTP; and finally, the last source of information was press people who were in Tuzla at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A little bit more and then we'll move on to other areas. Professionally, when you told us the other day that there was a process for investigating witnesses, and I summarise it a little so please correct me if I'm wrong, I thought you had said that the process was that one investigator would not investigate more than one witness who happens to be a survivor of the same event or massacre, as you called it.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is for the sake of avoiding what you previously named -- I don't remember the psychiatric term that you were using.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll remind you a little later.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. So it is just -- it's very simple. It's to avoid being under the influence of the information already provided by one of these witnesses, and then getting, let's say, influenced by this information later on when questioning the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: To preserve the integrity of the investigation, basically; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it's necessary so that it can be maintained at least at some level to give it some objectivity; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Otherwise, if you had done it with two witnesses, it would have been what I think you called biased; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not necessarily, because getting under influence of biased judgement is a question of personality. Some people are more subject to that than others. And you have understood that I don't put myself in the category of those who are easily subject to bias.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I understand. That's fine. We want to use your definition. It's to avoid being under the influence of the information already provided by one of these witnesses; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you had the other day what I call - I don't know how else to call it - but a cheat sheet of witnesses names and description and 65 ter numbers. Do you remember that, in your right breast pocket?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the same document that was provided to you by the Prosecutor, I have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not debating. He did give it to us, and we're grateful to him. It's not a question. But do you have that document?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely I have it on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, look, can we take it out so we can explore it a little bit?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Great. Thank you. My learned friend of the Prosecutor's Office, I apologise for having to give this, we kind of agreed that we're not going to reference the names of the individuals, rather their 65 ter number. I think you've done that, but just to remind you of that, and I'm sure you remember it; correct? Okay. Now, if I told you that you interviewed 65 ter number 41; do you see it? What's it say under his name for "description"?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orahovac survivor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And 65 ter number 38, which was, I think, PW-101 -- 110, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Orahovac survivor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then do you see the last one who doesn't have a 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: He was also an Orahovac survivor; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, do you remember, as you sit here, whether or not you interviewed these three survivors of Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were four survivors at Orahovac. One additional one --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: He's up on top there.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just don't have a statement from him, but we'll get to it.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think unfortunately he's the one who died recently. The Prosecutor might confirm. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Mr. Ruez, Mr. McCloskey is not going to testify. If you don't recall, tell us you don't recall. We'll flesh it out with him, I'm sure, later. If you remember something, share it with us, by all means.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So four survivors for Orahovac. I most probably had interviewed at least two of them. Maybe even three of them. Could be. You have the names on the statements of these four.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
