utterances.text: I do, actually. And what I want to do is -- it's my position that you interviewed all three of the survivors of Orahovac, and that, in fact, if you can reconcile for me -- or do you remember interviewing all three?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't, but it's fairly possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Number -- Witness PW-110, you interviewed him on at least two occasions, 20th of August, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, if I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the 13th of June, 1999. Witness number 41, you testified, 24 January, 1996. And witness who doesn't have a 65 ter number, who is the last one on the list, I believe; correct? Yes? The last one on the list, do you see him?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. That person you interviewed the 10th of August, 1995, and the 7th of July of 1996. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, help me reconcile your position earlier that in order to be thorough, complete, and objective, that you wouldn't interview the same witnesses from a same potential massacre because it would, as you say, maybe -- or how did you put it, influence? Influence and, the way I put it, compromise the integrity of the investigation. Can you reconcile that for me?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will. Two reasons for that. One point is that during the summer 1995, I already said that we were not so much in numbers. In fact, we were initially -- I mean, I was initially alone at the beginning. Then at the beginning of August, after returning from a short go and return to The Hague, I could have the assistance of one investigator, and at some point around the 10th -- 10 of August, a third -- I mean a second assistant arrived in the area. So when I say -- and not only that, sorry. Then, upon return after that summer in the area, there was no one in charge of the investigation aside myself. That lasted more than a year, nearly, since the first investigator attached, in fact, was attached in April 1996 and permanent staffing arrived only at the end of the year of 1996. So when I say that it's a better policy not to interview people from the same situation by only one person, it is a fact that it is also depending on the material possibility to do so. So that was not always the case, unfortunately, at the start of this investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We're always fighting budget problems ourselves, so I understand. Now, help me with this, though: In 1999, having -- since you had interviewed the same witness in 1996, don't you think it would have been prudent and objective and thorough to have another investigator, instead of confirm what the witness said by sending you again, that he would -- you would send another investigator in 1999 when you didn't have constraints, perhaps, with personnel or budget?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily for -- not necessarily. Depending on what was the need for the contact, if it was a need to re-contact the witness in order to show him, for example, photographs or a video, my view is that it was better that the person who took the picture and the video and who knew, therefore, the area would be the one who would present that material to the witness. So this is probably the reason why I re-contacted one or several of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Share with me, if you will, the process that you used as an investigator to verify certain information that was given to you by witnesses, key or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is very depending on the situation. But the main thing, especially during the summer 1995, as the war was ongoing, was the possibility to have access to the territory of the Republika Srpska. That was not the case in 1995. That started to become the case in 1996. So the first thing we were eager to do was to identify the locations of interest and transport ourselves to these locations in order to check the information and what could be done with the information, depending on what we would find on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't know that you answered my question, with all due respect, but I'd like to move on if we may. And I'll look at it again, and if you have, thank you. Just to jump around a little bit, because you're on this list we have, and the witnesses on the list, do you recall your testimony, sir, on the Krstic case, page 538, lines 13 through 21, I believe, and page 584, lines 3 through 6, and there you were discussing the Vuk Karadzic school. Just to put it in some context for you. Let me ask you this first: "Sir, isn't it true that the OTP and you," the collective "we" - I guess, right? - "do not have any survivor who stayed inside the Vuk Karadzic school."

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct not when we talk about the Vuk Karadzic complex but when we talk about the Vuk Karadzic school. We do not have a survivor who stayed inside the school, indeed. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And when we talk about thoroughness and completeness, you would have probably interviewed Witness 42, on this cheat sheet, as we -- as I call it, 65 ter number 42, and you would have verified that; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Witness 42.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: 42, you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, he was held at the so-called old school, the technical school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To be precise, in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Bratunac town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, is it true, sir, that you received the information regarding the Vuk Karadzic school that only one room was used for the detainees, if we can call them that, with all due respect?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of several meetings that I had with Mr. Miroslav Deronjic, if he is the one you refer to with this detailed information, after having, at initial stages, denied any knowledge about anything problematic that might have occurred in his town, he indeed, at one point of our relationship, disclosed during one interview that yes, indeed, the Vuk Karadzic school had been used, but at the end of the interview he modified slightly the information by being more precise and saying that only one school had been used -- one classroom, sorry, had been used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic, we need to have a break, either now or whenever it's convenient for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Whatever is the pleasure of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we'll have it now. Thank you. Twenty minutes. Twenty minutes. We'll try to recover a little bit of the lost ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, I'd like to, if we can, in the interests of time, move to another topic. Can we discuss the aerial images that is in the binder --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let me follow you on the other one, because this is not working again. All right. The LiveNote as such is not working, or at least in mine. It is connected so I don't know what's happening. Yes, go ahead, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd like to discuss the aerial images that is in the binder of 271 photos, if we may.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, by my count, there's -- 36 or so of the 271 photos in that binder were of aerial images; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't count them, but you are certainly correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When did you request them?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer would have to be detailed, because it was not a request that was made in one blow. The requests were made in the process of compiling information that could confirm or infirm the declarations made by the witnesses. So, in fact, each time we encountered a situation where we believed aerial imagery could be useful in order to find out more about the events that were disclosed to us, we were making a request through the US embassy. So for most of the crime scenes we are talking about, it was, let's say, a discovery after a discovery. Until one point that was, as I said, early 1997, when, having found secondary mass graves in Zeleni Jadar, the findings were confirmed by imagery. The imagery even enabled us to find more sites than we were aware of at Zeleni Jadar. And then all the other secondary mass grave sites were provided to us by US government pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay, thanks. So early 1997; correct? That's the answer, basically.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the moment when we received, let's say, on the initiative of the provider, this material. Before that we were the ones requesting the pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And how did you request it? What mode did you use? Written form, telephonic, electronic? Which?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm going to object to that as going to the processes and procedures --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we need to know this, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Apart from the --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't want to debate it but -- I don't, and that's why I'm asking the witness. But I'll move on, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And when was the last time that you received such aerial images that we're discussing that's in this binder in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The very last one might be the picture of the disturbance of the Kozluk site.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just give me a year and a month, if you remember, and we'll look at it in a few months, to the extent that you recall it.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that case, that would be 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And no pictures after 1998; correct? No aerial images -- I'm sorry, no aerial images requested or received after 1998; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could be more specific, because, as we know, he left in 2001. So that would leave a false impression in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I beg to differ with my learned friend, but if the last time he knows that they were received was in 2001, then it wouldn't leave a false impression because we know he left in 2001. If he says 1998 or 1999, then I think we can put it together. He can just tell us whatever year it is. This is really preliminary, Your Honour, and I'm hoping to get to the question, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The understanding is that whatever answer he gives it will be limited for the period 1998 until the 7th April, 2001, when he left.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So as far as I know, and to the best of my recollection, the last one received were probably requested for the preparation of the trial of General Krstic. It was, for example, one picture of Batkovic prison camp. And that would be 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. So I still don't what "infirm" means but I'm going to look it up and try to figure that out. You were asking and requesting these documents in order to confirm your investigation; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only in order to confirm, but mainly in order to enable us to continue this investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But to confirm, nonetheless, in part; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. Mr. Ruez has explained what he means by "confirm" and "infirm" repeatedly, and I think the Court understands, and it's a bit of an adaptation to the English language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Objection sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, are you family with the acronym NIMA, N-I-M-A?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There will be an objection, I bet.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You know ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do not represent the interests of the United States, but if we go into this further, I would need to ask the United States to be present.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I briefly respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let me confer with my colleagues because I must express my ignorance about what the acronym stands for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start from here, because this is -- presents itself as a delicate matter, in a way: Can we know what NIMA, the acronym, stands for, to start with?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no objection with Mr. Ostojic telling us, but if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Maybe then I come to your point. But for the time being, I mean, we all profess our ignorance as to the meaning of this acronym, or what this acronym stands for.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I would just ask, Mr. President and Your Honours, just to be patient for two seconds and we'll get to it. I just want to know if he knew what it meant. If he knows and then he does want to tell us, we'll get to it in the next two minutes, I promise. And if not, I'll tell you. If you want to know now, I'll tell you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's this mystery? You tell us because it will help us decide ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to tell it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll tell him if you won't. It's not a secret society.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's the National Imaging and Mapping Agency, NIMA, National Imaging and Mapping Agency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So he now knows about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But coming -- I don't know what the series of questions that you have in mind are, but please do keep in mind that we have Rule 70 here that restricts us considerably; and that if, at any time, there is a request from the Prosecution to have either the go-ahead from the United States government -- either the go-ahead from the United States government or the presence of United States government officials here, as has been the case in practically every case I have been involved in, then that would be granted, because that is the practice and the law of this Tribunal. But still I don't want to jump the gun. I don't know what your questions are going to be. At the moment Mr. McCloskey stands up and objects to us proceeding with that line of questions without the presence of the United States government, or consulate, we'll stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Forewarned is forearmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Out of these 36 or so aerial images that we saw, sir, I've seen some - if I can use the word "inconsistent" - some inconsistencies in them. For example, some have the place, some have the place and the date, some have a place, date, and time, and yet others have a place, date, time, and specification within that place. Do you remember those when we went through them the other day or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why do you call those inconsistencies?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why do you call them inconsistencies?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Because all of them do not contain all the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They are not inconsistent. "Inconsistent" means something else, at least to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Different, may I use that? I'm leading to a different point so maybe I'm thinking a little ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: They're different in some way?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some way, yes. The markings are not always the same, depending on the pictures we're looking at, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know why they're different? Do you know why in some there's a specification of a place and in some there's a time and in others there's not even a time or a date?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We're getting into that area, again. Your Honour, both Mr. Ruez and I are under obligation to our agreement with the United States, and under Rule 70, the law of this Tribunal. As you're aware, these documents, while they've been around for a long time, are extremely serious documents, and the United States, I know, takes it very seriously. And we are right at -- we are asking Mr. Ruez to provide information that is -- that may be United States' information, and I -- if you want to get a lawyer from the United States here, okay, but I think we're really on slippery ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our position is a very simple one, and it emerges from the Rule itself that has just been referred to by Mr. McCloskey: Any questions that you would like to put on these images provided to the OTP, or to the Tribunal, let's put it like that, pursuant to Rule 70, would require the presence of at least officers from the United States government here, and the witness will answer the question if they agree that he can answer the question. Otherwise you will have the legal impediment that you are aware of, that I don't need to explain. You're all aware of it. So if you want to pursue this series of questions, I suggest that you stop for the time being and jump to a next series of questions and leave this until we have made -- concluded arrangements for US government officials to be present.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I respect that, and I will -- if I may be permitted just to ask about one specific photo, at the very least, out of those 36 or so in the binder of 271, obviously, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then I will see what the protection of the Prosecution will be, and we will decide either -- the same as we have already told you or differently if it's -- there's a need to decide differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I have many questions in this area, but I'm going to limit it to this photo, based on the Court's ruling. Thank you, if I may proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If you can look at photo 236, I believe. It's in the binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we don't have the binder, Mr. Ostojic. We need to wait until it shows up on the -- on e-court. Otherwise, if it is readily available -- yes, okay. We can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you have it yet, Mr. Ruez?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have numbers on my pages, so if someone could show it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm glad to hear that, because neither do I. I had to number them.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you see it now, Mr. Ruez?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you see that this photo, number 236. It's not a secret where I got the acronym or the words -- the words for the acronym NIMA; right? It's on that photo; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: This is your binder that you created and you gave to the Prosecutor who gave it to the Court and to the Defence lawyers; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, in this one it has the actual symbol of an agency; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it has.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And no other document has that; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, have you found any in that binder of 271 that have that symbol?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you are right. I never noticed that point. This is the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about on the bottom right-hand corner of that photo? Do you see what that inscription is?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Don't answer what it is, just tell me if you know what it is, if I may ask that.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. We'll come back to that, I hope, soon. Do you know why there's a difference in -- in this photo, why there would be a symbol on the description of the place and the specification of the picture and on the right-hand side what seems to be a digitalised or an inscription of some kind? Do you know why this photo has that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: My concern is that some of the photos, for example, didn't have the date and they had a box that still remained. And my question to you is: Do you know who removed the date, if at all?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: On some of the pictures that I used, not as such, but in order to talk about the different events that -- in an area shown by this imagery but that was not initially designed to present that situation, I am the one who erased the dates so that we keep only, let's say, what can be seen on the picture but not the reason why it was given to us. I take one example --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You don't have to give us an example, if you don't mind. That's what I thought too, Mr. Ruez, that in fact you manipulated these pictures by adding or placing certain dates or times on these aerial images; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not true. As I said, all the markings in white on these pictures in the entire binder are US government markings. All of the markings that are in colour are markings that I added myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But when you removed white, that was something that you removed; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. When there was a use of the pictures but not in connection with the reason why they were provided, I erased the date, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you told us when you started your direct examination that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You told us, I believe, when you started your direct examination that you have a collection, I think, of 2.000 photographs.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We've seen 271 of them here. Those are yours; correct? Or ...

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What happened to the other 90-some per cent -- 80-something per cent, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are in the evidence room with ERN numbers, at least for those who have a direct connection with the investigation, certainly not those that we can call "touristic pictures."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we're not interested in touristic pictures either, quite candidly. But do you know, out of the 2.000 or so collection that you have or had, do you know how many of these, other than these 36, are aerial images?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I gave a number of 2.000 and something, I was not talking about aerial imagery. I was talking about photographs I took myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That very well may be true, and I apologise if I misunderstood it. I thought you were talking about the binder that we have. So tell -- help me with this: How many aerial images do you know were in the possession of the Office of the Prosecution when you were their lead investigator?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have a list of all of them, but I don't remember by heart how many we received.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if it is more than 36?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for sure. I didn't use all of them for the sake of this presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How many more than 36?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not much more. All those that were relevant to the crime scenes we exposed during this session have been used. I didn't use some related to the situation in Potocari. I didn't use all those connected with secondary sites, since what was shown is aerial photography and not every single grave. So we have at least one picture per secondary grave, and a few like this that I spared in order to win time for the presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sorry. How many more than 36, is really all I wanted to know. Do you think it's more than 50? If you can't recall, that's fine. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we count the photographs showing secondary sites, I would say less than 40, since there are at least 30 of these secondary sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, in your efforts to be objective and a thorough and a complete investigator, did you ask the United States to give you aerial imagery of Potocari, for example, on July 12th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have one picture for July 12, and we have also one for July 13 of Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about July 11th, 1995? Did you ever request that the United States give you an aerial image of the situation in Potocari on July 11th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is getting into an area of Rule 70 sensitivity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic, we are unanimously in agreement here that this question should not be put in the absence of US government representatives, and with their consent.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. I'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, did you request a picture from the United States government of the column that was leaving Susnjari and going towards Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, we fall in the same -- this is exactly the same category.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. If I may -- so I understand, perhaps I didn't understand Your Honour. I thought that question, this whole area, if I'm restricted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it's not the whole area. Mr. Ostojic, we will let you put several questions that the witness felt comfortable with answering, and Mr. McCloskey, although I could see him toying with the idea of jumping up, failed to do so. So you were allowed to proceed. But you know what the limitations of Rule 70 are. If Mr. McCloskey stands up and says: This is an area covered by the agreement that we have -- the restrictions that we have from the United States government, we have to comply. We get the officials, and if there is no objection, the question will be asked and answered; if there is an objection, the question will not be answered. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. I just want to reserve my right to question Mr. Ruez when we reach that period of time on these and similar issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if the rest of the questions that you may have for today - we only got 20 minutes left - are along the same lines, in other words, let's stop here, it will give time to Mr. McCloskey to communicate with the US embassy here, but they always have someone there, and they will try to have two officials present tomorrow. They usually comply within a very short time, and you will find two legal experts sitting in the courtroom here with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Whatever the Court's pleasure. I can move on or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not a question of pleasure. I'm quite uncomfortable, actually. It's not a pleasure at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a question of, you need to understand that if we have this wall erected, you have to comply.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand the parameters. I'll move away from the aerial images. I understand that area, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go to whatever other area you want to ask the witness about. In the meantime, please do confirm to Mr. McCloskey that you require the presence of US government representatives here so that he can start making the arrangements, because there is a protocol to be followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. If I can just confirm it here, in case I lose him at this hour. I'd like them here, and if we can continue tomorrow, that would be fantastic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I haven't been able to get them to respond that quickly, Judge. I'll try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you don't succeed, that will not be the end of the world, Mr. McCloskey, because there are still five other Defence teams that need to put questions. If necessary, we'll have Mr. Ostojic finish the rest of the cross-examination that has got nothing to do with this aerial images, photos, and then can come back to his series of question when is the US government is in a position to provide us with the -- its personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I can briefly -- perhaps this will help. Questions about photos we have and whether or not we asked for it or not, I think, is okay. Questions about photos that we don't have and speculation on why we don't have them, or why -- that is definitely in a murkier area that is off limits. I think the Court under -- understands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, Mr. McCloskey - just a second - the last question asked by Mr. Ostojic may be relevant in a sense. I'm having difficulty finding the page number. If you could help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Page 77, line 8, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I'd like to make sure that it is not that we are prohibiting you from asking the question. If you need to -- if you find the question necessary, we can proceed with the presence of the US lawyers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The last question is --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, Your Honour. I was just mistaken when Mr. President said that question cannot be asked, and I thought he just wanted me to list out the question. But I understand the ruling now and I'm prepared to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the last question was, in case Mr. McCloskey wants to go back on his question, Mr. Ruez, answer your question said: "We have one picture for July 12th, and we have also one for July 13." And then you ask him: "How about July 11, 1995? Did you ever request that the United States give you an aerial image of the situation in Potocari on July 11th, 1995?" Do you maintain your opposition to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not giving anything away --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Finished. Discussion is over. You will be able to put that question in the presence of the US government, unless there is an opposition to it. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I wish to intervene in this debate because it is something that affects more than one of the co-accused in this case. I believe it is important for us to go back to the basics when we deal with Rule 70. If we go back to the basics, I'm not even sure that what we're talking about right now is covered by this Rule. When we look at Rule 70, once the Prosecution elects -- the Prosecution has received information in a confidential by a provider. Fine. Nothing we can do about that. And they can even not disclose it to the Defence. That's Rule 70. Then at some point in time, with the consent of the provider, the Prosecution can elect to use that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me cut you short --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Once --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me cut you short. Please read paragraph (D) of Rule 70: "If the Prosecutor calls a witness to introduce in evidence any information provided under this rule, the Trial Chamber may not compel that witness to answer any question relating to the information or its origin if the witness declines to answer on grounds of confidentiality."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know here if the Prosecution is answering or the witness is answering. I haven't heard the witness refuse to answer any question. He might be the investigator. He hasn't refused once to answer any question. He is the investigation -- the investigator in this case. My colleague is quite appropriately asking him: Did you make a request for a picture to so and so. He could say: Did you make a picture -- did you make a request to Judge so-and-so for a picture, and the investigator should be able to answer: Yes, I did make a request, or no, I did not make a request. But what is wrong with that question? I really fail to see how it falls under the umbrella of Rule 70. Because the investigator is talk about his investigation, and we are here to investigate into his investigation, to see how it was conducted, what was the methodology, why did he ask for this picture, why he did not have any other means to get the same information. If he had to go through a process of asking the government of the United States for confidential information, that must have been a reason for that. I think it's important for the Trial Chamber to know what these reasons are and for the Defence to know what these reasons are. We have to know what were the limits imposed on this investigator when he was trying to investigate so that we can prepare the case for the Defence. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you've got it all wrong, Mr. Bourgon. Basically the witness is not testifying on documents that he himself procured with some kind of agreement with the US government. These were procured by the Office of the Prosecutor, and they are the property of the Office of the Prosecutor, in a way. And if there are restrictions from the US government, I can't -- I can't ask Mr. McCloskey to go beyond a certain amount of information, because that would, in itself, be a violation of Rule 70 itself. So, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As you recall in direct testimony, I made reference, and Mr. Ruez confirmed, that we are allowed under this agreement to refer to this material as imagery, US surveillance systems and the information on it. And as for anything else, they may be fine. But I doubt it, based on my knowledge of some of this, and I just want -- as I know your court -- if we could have the United States representing the United States here. That's all I ask. We need to really be careful with our Rule 70 agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I would definitely not expose the Prosecution to a possible violation of the agreement reached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think exactly the decision is on this matter: We'll definitely adjourn until we get the representatives of the US government here, and then you will be able to proceed, to the extent that it will be able to -- possible to proceed. But, of course, you'll have every opportunity to put all the questions that you like, Mr. Ostojic. You and the rest. Incidentally, if there are other Defence teams that will be dealing with the question of these aerial images supplied or provided by the US government, please notify the Prosecutor -- Prosecution accordingly so that arrangements are, again, put in place with the US government. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I certainly do indeed intend to go into the aerial imagery. If I can make a suggestion: What is missing in this debate is that the Prosecutor -- Prosecution has obtained consent to use these exhibits as evidence. Now, the provider has also imposed some limits. We don't know what these limits are. If a representative of the US government is not able to come up tomorrow, at least my colleague should provide to this Chamber, in a confidential manner, in an ex parte manner, if need be, what exact limits were placed on these exhibits. Here we are in public session, looking at pictures. Justice must be done, but just must be seen to be done. I'm sure the public out there surely does not understand why we have a picture and that we cannot speak about a picture like this when it's been provided by the Government of the United States. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Back to the point, Mr. Bourgon. You've twisted it in a way which does not represent the reality. We have never said that there is a prohibition of discussing these pictures. These pictures can be discussed within the parameters of the agreement that exists between the US government and this Tribunal. We can only know what these parameters are if -- either if Mr. McCloskey obtains the permission of the US government to tell us, or else if the US government officials come over and tell us themselves, failing which you will have to live with the reality of Rule 70; and only those questions that will get the okay of the US government representatives will be allowed to be put and answered. This is the position. And it's not an innovation. I mean, I've had it in Oric, I've had it in Brdjanin, I've had it ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will adjourn very soon. The position is as follows: You will make arrangements, as necessary, for the presence in the courtroom of officials of the US government. In the meantime, as has been the case in other cases, that at least I am aware of, whenever there has been an agreement between the US government and the Tribunal in relation to either the testimony of a person or the use of particular documents provided by the US government, usually the parameters of the conditions -- the parameters of the agreement or the conditions are incorporated in a written document. In other words, if you have a communication, official communication, by the US government -- from the US government authorising you, under Rule 70, to make use of these aerial images in proceedings, in criminal proceedings, under conditions 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, we would like to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't think that should be a problem. I've reviewed that before coming to court, and I don't think the US has a problem with that. But frankly, this has not come up before. We are a bit surprised by this. This is the first time I've seen a challenge that's getting behind the aerial images. It would be nice to have a little bit of notice, especially dealing with the United States. But we'll do our best to get them in here and get you that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate that. On the other hand, Defence teams, you need to be pragmatic and practical, and now that this has arisen, I can't guarantee that the US government officials would be able to be here tomorrow morning. So if that is not possible, the options that remain are the following: Mr. Ostojic, you have the floor, you may continue with your cross-examination on other matters; you can be followed by other Defence teams on other matters; and any Defence team that wishes to question the witness on the aerial images in a way that requires the presence of the US government officials will do so when we have them available here in the courtroom. All right? Clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I have -- I have two small points, Your Honour, if I may. I just want --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Very quickly, because I don't want to keep the staff more than 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I don't think, with all due respect, and honestly I'm speaking, I don't think these questions are covered within a parameter and that's why I asked for them, I'm not looking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not for you to say, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Secondly, if I may, Your Honour, I think it's important that we examine the issue, as I mentioned the other day, of waiver. And I think that that's the issue that, if we examine these photographs and all issues relating and questions relating to these aerial images -- I'm sorry, aerial images, will help us to understand that if they produce them and they know that they are going to be used in an exhibit that this witness created, that this witness brought to court, I think waiver is an important issue. So I would like to just add that, if I may, to the issues that the Court may discuss.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We stand adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00. Yes, Mr. Meek. You disagree with your colleague?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Of course, I always agree with him. This has nothing to do with that. My colleague Mr. Lazarevic told me that on the website it showed the ground floor is closed from 7 to 9 tomorrow to take out asbestos. So I'm wondering, if that's the case, how do we get in the building?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. I have a status conference at 8.00. So I will face the problem before you do, if that will be a problem. I don't think there should be. I don't know where you come in from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, there is a ground floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is a ground floor from this level and a ground floor at the other level. If you come from the main entrance, there is no asbestos that is being removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
